Stage
entries.doc:
The engine's front door: one rigged creature (or a scene) on a canvas, drawn
by `SplatWorld` through three.js's WebGPU renderer, which falls back to
WebGL 2 where a browser has no WebGPU. Every blob is moved by its bones on
the GPU, so a creature can have hundreds of thousands. It plays a clip or a
poser, orbits, picks bones, draws pixel art and bakes sprite sheets.

  const stage = await Stage.start(canvas)
  stage.setActor(makeFox(20000), recordClip('trot', ...))

On blobscape.dev it is the Creature page's view (`CreatureStage`) and every
engine experiment's.

`offscreen` draws into a render target and copies each frame to a 2D canvas
on request: headless test browsers can render WebGPU but not show it.

modules.title: SplatWorld: every blob in one three.js object

entries.name: Actor
entries.doc:
Blobscape's splat engine: one mesh that draws every blob of every object in a
scene, so objects that overlap (stems in a vase, a fox in long grass) sort
against each other blob by blob, instead of object by object.

Every blob hangs on bones. A still object is one bone; a creature is a
skeleton. Each frame:

1. deform (compute): each blob's center and shape go from its rest pose to the
   world through its bones, as `skinBlob` in rig.ts does on the CPU;
2. sort (compute): every blob in the scene by depth, one counting sort;
3. draw: one instanced quad per blob, projected and shaded as in 3DGS.

It draws through three.js's WebGPURenderer, so it shares a depth buffer and a
camera with ordinary three.js meshes. On the WebGL backend the deform and sort
run on the CPU and the result is uploaded; the drawing is the same.

The projection and shading follow three.js's `GaussianSplat` (MIT), which in
turn follows the 3DGS paper; what's new here is the shared sort and skinning.

entries.name: Blobs
entries.doc:
A list of Gaussian blobs, kept as flat typed arrays (one entry per blob) so a
scene of tens of thousands stays cheap to copy, undo and hand to the GPU.

Each blob is the five kinds of number (14 values) a 3D Gaussian splat is made of:
a center, three scales (standard deviations along its own axes), a rotation
(unit quaternion x, y, z, w), a color and an opacity. Colors are stored as
given to Spark (0–1 per channel), which draws them as sRGB.

entries.name: Vec3
entries.code: type Vec3 = [number, number, number];

entries.name: Bone
entries.doc:
A skeleton: bones in a tree, each placed by its head in the rest pose (world
space, no rest rotation) and posed by a local rotation about its head plus an
optional offset. Bone 0 is usually the root; a still object in a scene is just
a skeleton of one bone.

`update()` turns the pose into what the skinning pass needs per bone: the skin
matrix (posed world × inverse rest, column-major 4×4), its rotation as a
quaternion, and its uniform scale. A bone's scale carries down to its
children, as in glTF.

entries.name: packWeights
entries.doc:
Four weights to four bytes summing to exactly 255, so a blob never shrinks

rounding leaves over goes to the largest weight. All zero means the first bone.
entries.code: function packWeights(w: ArrayLike<number>, o: number): number;

entries.name: SkinMode

entries.name: skinBlob
entries.doc:
Moves one blob by its bones. Positions blend the skin matrices linearly (as
every engine does). The blob's shape then follows one of two rules:

- 'linear': its covariance is pushed through the blended 3×3 matrix. A blend of
  two rotations is not a rotation, so a blob on a twisting joint gets squashed.
- 'quat': its rotation is the weighted average of the bone rotations
  (quaternions sign-aligned, summed, renormalized) and its scale the weighted
  average scale, so the blob only ever turns, never flattens.

Writes the world center (3) and covariance [xx, xy, xz, yy, yz, zz] (6).

entries.name: skinCenters
entries.doc:
Moves only the centers of many blobs, fast: what the sort needs on the CPU
when the GPU does the rest of the skinning. No allocation per blob.

- `src`: rest centers as vec4s, with each blob's first bone (its actor's
  offset into `bones`) in w;
- `skin`: two words per blob, four joint bytes then four weight bytes summing to 255;
- `bones`: 20 floats per bone, the first 16 its column-major skin matrix.

Writes xyz into `out` (3 floats per blob). Matches `skinBlob`'s center.

entries.name: MixMove
Mixer
entries.doc:
Plays moves and crossfades between them. `play(name, fade)` brings one move
up to full weight over `fade` seconds while every other fades out; `update(dt)`
moves the clocks and weights on; `apply(sk)` poses the skeleton as the
weighted blend. Weights always sum to 1 while anything plays, so a blend is
never a shrunken pose.

Each move keeps its own time, and `speed` scales a move's clock: a walk can
keep pace with the ground while the idle under it breathes on.

modules.title: Reaching and feet on the ground
modules.doc:
Reaching for things: inverse kinematics on our skeletons, the part of a
mesh engine's animation tools (three.js's `CCDIKSolver`, a game engine's
foot IK) that creatures need most.

- `twoBoneIK` bends a limb of two bones (thigh and shin, arm and forearm)
  so its end lands on a point, keeping the knee on the side it bends now;
- `lookAt` turns one bone so a direction it carries points at a place;
- `plantFeet` lays a walk over uneven ground: hips down to the lower foot,
  each leg bent to its own patch of ground, each foot tilted to the slope;
- `hipDrop` and `stepLegs` put feet where a footstep planner (steps.ts) says.

Bones here have no rest rotation, so a bone's world turn is the product of
the local ones up its chain (`worldQuat`), and changing a bone's world turn
means setting its local turn to parent⁻¹ · wanted.

modules.title: Footsteps
modules.doc:
Footstep planning: instead of a walk clip moving the legs and the feet being pinned to the ground
after, each foot keeps a spot on the ground and only leaves it to step. A foot steps when its spot has fallen
too far from where it would stand under the body now (`reach`), aiming up to `reach` ahead of the body's motion, so
one planner walks, turns on the spot, sidesteps, backs up and stops with every foot still where it landed.
Feet in one `group` step together (a trot's diagonal pair); only one group is ever in the air, and the group
furthest behind goes first. Pure, plain numbers: the same motion gives the same steps.

modules.title: Loose parts that swing
modules.doc:
Loose parts that swing after the body: tails, ears, cloaks, plaits. Each
chain is a run of bones, each the child of the one before; its points are
every bone's head and the last bone's tail. The first point is pinned where
the body carries it, and the rest are pulled loosely toward where the move
puts them (`follow`, a compliance: bigger is looser), so they lag, swing and
settle (xpbd.ts). Afterwards each bone is turned to point at the next point,
so the move still shapes the part and the swing rides on top.

  const s = new Swing(sk, FOX_SWING)   // once
  ...pose the move, place the creature...
  s.update(sk, dt)                     // turns the chains' bones

Pure and tested.

modules.title: Cloth solver
modules.doc:
A small position-based dynamics solver (XPBD, "small steps" form: many
substeps, one pass over the constraints in each), for cloth and hair hung
on a rig. Points carry an inverse mass (0 = pinned, moved by the caller);
links keep two points at a length, goals pull a point toward where the
animation puts it, and capsules push points out of the body. Compliance is
the inverse of stiffness: 0 is rigid.

It always steps by `STEP`, carrying what's left of a frame to the next, so
the same frames give the same motion and a recorded loop can be played back.
Pure and tested.

entries.name: MorphTarget
entries.doc:
Morphs (blend shapes) for blobs: a second way to move them, beside bones.
A bone carries its blobs rigidly. A morph gives every blob its own small
change, and a slider says how much of it to take, so a cheek can puff or a
mouth can curl with no bone at all.

A mesh morph only moves points. A blob has a shape too, so each target holds
two things per blob:

- `delta`: how far the center moves (3 numbers), as a mesh morph does;
- `grad`: how the surface round the blob stretches and turns (9 numbers),
  the change in the morph's local 3×3 map, J − I.

With weights w the center is p + Σ w·delta and the blob's covariance goes
through J = I + Σ w·grad, as Σ′ = J Σ Jᵀ. Both add up, so morphs mix, run
backward and overshoot the way mesh morphs do, and Σ′ is always a real
covariance whatever the weights.

A morph is a straight line. A part that must travel round something (an
eyelid over an eye) gets in-between `targets`, reached in turn as the weight
goes from 0 to 1.

entries.name: PickHit
entries.doc:
Picking: which blob of which actor is under a pointer, as the actor stands
posed right now, and which bone and part it belongs to.

Each blob's bones move it by a blend of their skin matrices. That blend, M,
carries the blob's rest ellipsoid to where it is drawn (exactly, in the
'linear' rule; to within the rounding of a joint in 'quat'), and a straight
line through M is still a straight line with the same distances along it.
So the ray is taken back into the blob's rest frame through M⁻¹ and tested
against the rest blob there, with `rayHit`, as a still scene is.

entries.name: Shape
entries.doc:
A voxel builder for pixel-art scenes: shapes given as distance functions are
cut into a grid, and every grid cell on a shape's surface becomes one small,
nearly solid blob, a disc lying flat on the surface. Drawn small and snapped to a palette (pixelPass.ts)
a scene of these reads as chunky pixel art with real depth.

Where body.ts scatters flat blobs over a creature's skin and blends them
between bones, this fills a regular grid and hangs each part on one bone, so
parts move rigidly (a lamp turns, a boat bobs) and the grid stays crisp.

Light is baked into the colors: one sun, an ambient floor, and shadows cast
by every part on every other, found by marching from each blob toward the
sun through the scene's shapes in the rest pose. `glow` parts keep their
color and cast no shadow. Three optional touches a pixel artist would paint
(all off unless the light asks): `ramp` turns shade cool and light warm
instead of only darker, `crevice` darkens what is shut in by other surfaces,
and `wear` lightens edges. A part's `grime` collects where it is shut in.

entries.name: VoxelPart
Glass
entries.doc:
A surface you see into and that mirrors what is over it, baked for one place to look from (the spec's `eye`, the
scene's camera): pixel mode cuts anything faint, so instead of being drawn see-through, each cell takes the color
of what lies behind it on the line from the eye (`see`) and of what its mirror line meets (`mirror`, stronger at a
glancing look, as on real water). Seen from far off the scene's own view it is a painting of glass, not glass.

entries.name: Ink
entries.doc:
Inked detail: the surface is taken in blocks of 4×4 cells (one picture pixel each in pixel mode), and a share of
the blocks (`amount`) each carry one small mark of the kind, picked, turned and flipped at random per block and with
the blocks of each row shifted, so a big wall never shows a repeat. `color` is the ink; left out, a darker step of
the paint under it.

entries.code: type InkKind = 'hatch' | 'stipple' | 'cracks' | 'grain' | 'tufts' | 'scales';

entries.name: Cover
entries.doc:
Something laid over the whole scene once it is cut: `snow` settles on tops that the sky can reach, `moss` creeps
over shut-in and up-turned faces in patches, `dust` lies thin on every upturned face, under cover or not.

entries.name: LooseBlob
entries.doc:
A blob placed as it is, not cut from a shape: soft, faint things in the air such as mist or a beam of light. Kept
under LOOSE_MAX opacity, so pixel mode's map of parts never takes one for a surface.

entries.name: Beam
entries.doc:
A beam of light falling through the scene, as from a window or a gap in the leaves: surfaces inside it that face
back up it are lit by its color, on top of the sun, so the beam shows where it lands.

entries.name: LOOSE_MAX
entries.doc: The most a loose blob may cover: under the engine's PART_CUT, so it never shows in the map of parts.

entries.name: cone
entries.doc: A rounded cone from a (radius ra) to b (radius rb); equal radii make a capsule.
entries.code: function cone(a: Vec3, b: Vec3, ra: number, rb?: number): Shape;

entries.name: cylinder
entries.doc: A upright cylinder with flat ends, from y0 to y1; `r1` tapers it.
entries.code: function cylinder(c: [x: number, z: number], y0: number, y1: number, r0: number, r1?: number): Shape;

entries.name: torus
entries.doc: A ring lying flat (about the y axis): `R` to the middle of the tube, `r` the tube's radius.
entries.code: function torus(c: Vec3, R: number, r: number): Shape;

entries.name: roof
entries.doc: A roof: a ridge along x at `top`, sloping down to `y0` at `hz` either side.
entries.code: function roof(c: [x: number, z: number], y0: number, top: number, hx: number, hz: number): Shape;

entries.name: union
entries.code: function union(...s: Shape[]): Shape;

entries.name: tighten
entries.doc:
A shape whose distance can overstate by up to 1/k − 1 of itself (a ragged edge, an overhang the side distance
doesn't see) made honest for the sun march: exact within `near` of the surface, where cells are placed, and
scaled by k beyond it, so a step never passes through.
entries.code: function tighten(s: Shape, k: number, near?: number): Shape;

entries.name: many
entries.code: function many(shapes: Shape[]): Shape;

entries.name: orientedBox
entries.doc:
A box turned any way: `axes` are its three edge directions (unit length, square to each other) and `half` its half
size along each. Fallen bricks, leaning posts, rails between them.
entries.code: function orientedBox(c: Vec3, axes: [Vec3, Vec3, Vec3], h: Vec3, round?: number): Shape;

entries.name: BlendKind
entries.doc: How a `blend` meets where its shapes touch: a rounded fillet, a flat bevel, or a run of little steps.
entries.code: type BlendKind = 'smooth' | 'chamfer' | 'stairs';

entries.name: blend
entries.doc: Shapes joined so the seam between them is filled in: `r` is how far the fillet, bevel or stairs reach.
entries.code: function blend(kind: BlendKind, r: number, shapes: Shape[], steps?: number): Shape;

entries.name: lathe
entries.doc:
A turned shape, as from a lathe: `profile` is [radius, height] pairs from the bottom up, standing on `c`, and the
outline is spun about the upright axis through it. Vases, bells, bottles, chess pieces, lamp posts.
entries.code: function lathe(c: Vec3, profile: [number, number][]): Shape;

entries.name: sweep
entries.doc: A tube along a path of points, `r0` thick at the start and `r1` at the end: vines, pipes, rails, a dragon's tail.
entries.code: function sweep(path: Vec3[], r0: number, r1?: number): Shape;

entries.name: LETTERS
entries.doc: The 3×5 letters `pixelText` knows, top row first.
entries.code: const LETTERS: Record<string, string>;

entries.name: pixelText
entries.doc:
Words in blocky 3×5 letters (`LETTERS`; lower case is read as upper), `size` tall and `depth` thick, centered on
`at` and reading along +x, or along -z when `facing` is 'x'. A letter needs about five grid cells of height to read.
entries.code: function pixelText(at: Vec3, text: string, size: number, depth: number, facing?: 'z' | 'x'): Shape;

entries.name: letterGrid
entries.doc:
A model drawn as letters: `layers` from the bottom up, each a list of rows from the back (-z) to the front, each
row a string read along +x; any character but '.' or a space fills a cube `size` across. Standing on `at`, centered
on it across. `letterAt` says which letter a point is in, so a paint can color the model by letter.

entries.name: cut
entries.doc: `a` with `b` cut out of it.
entries.code: function cut(a: Shape, b: Shape): Shape;

entries.name: displace
entries.doc: A shape pushed in or out by `f(x, y, z)` world units: ripples, rough rock. `reach` is the most it moves.
entries.code: function displace(s: Shape, f: (x: number, y: number, z: number) => number, reach: number): Shape;

entries.name: coverAt
entries.doc:
How much of a cover lies on a surface point, 0–1. `open` is its openness (moss wants it low) and `sky` how much
of the sky straight up it sees (snow wants it high); each is only asked for when the kind needs it.
entries.code: function coverAt(cover: Cover, p: Vec3, n: Vec3, spacing: number, open: () => number, sky: () => number): number;

entries.name: bakedColor
entries.doc:
A surface color under the baked light. `shade` is how bright (0 to LIT_MAX), `lit` how much straight sun it takes
(0–1). With `ramp` the color doesn't only darken: shade turns its hue toward violet and gains a little chroma in the
middle tones, full sun leans warm, and even a gray goes cool in shadow, so a palette's cool darks get picked over its
browns. `lift` lightens it (a worn edge). Never brighter than LIT_MAX, which keeps it under pixel mode's glow line.
entries.code: function bakedColor(base: Vec3, shade: number, lit: number, ramp: number, lift?: number): Vec3;

entries.name: buildVoxels
entries.doc:
Builds the scene's blobs, skin and skeleton. Cells sit on one grid shared by
every part (multiples of `spacing` from the origin), so parts line up, and
the same spec always gives the same blobs.
entries.code: function buildVoxels(spec: VoxelSpec): Built;

entries.name: SculptPart
entries.doc:
Creatures cut the way the pixel scenes are (voxel.ts): shapes given as
distance functions, one solid disc per surface cell, sun and cast shadows
baked in. What a scene does not need and a creature does is bending: here
every cell is weighted to the bones named on its part by distance, as
body.ts weights its blobs, so a neck or a tail curves without a seam.

Parts in one `group` are treated as one solid: a cell buried inside a
neighbor is never made. Give a part its own group when it swings clear of
the rest (a jaw, a wing), or what it uncovers would be missing.

entries.name: SculptSpec
Sculpted
DISC
entries.doc:
A creature's discs are wider than a scene's (voxel.ts `disc`): a creature is seen as blobs, without pixel mode's
alpha cut, and at the scene's size its far side showed through between them.
entries.code: const DISC = 0.75;

entries.name: buildSculpt
entries.doc: Cuts the creature on a grid of `spacing`.
entries.code: function buildSculpt(spec: SculptSpec, spacing: number): Sculpted;

entries.name: sculptToCount
entries.doc:
Cuts the creature at the spacing that gives about `count` blobs. Cells go
roughly as 1 / spacing², but not exactly (thin parts are fattened to the
grid), so it measures twice: a coarse cut, then one nearer the answer, each
a fraction of the final cut's cost. `make` is handed the spacing so thin
parts can be kept at least a cell thick.
entries.code: function sculptToCount(make: (spacing: number) => SculptSpec, count: number, probe?: number): Sculpted;

entries.name: toCount
entries.doc: `cut` at the spacing that gives about `count` blobs, for anything cut on a grid (a sculpt, a scene's creature).

entries.name: joinBuilt
entries.doc: One creature from two builds on the same bones (a sculpted body and a fuzzy flame, say): `b`'s blobs follow `a`'s.

entries.name: smooth
entries.doc: Shapes melted into each other over a distance `k`, so a neck runs into a chest without a crease.
entries.code: function smooth(k: number, ...s: Shape[]): Shape;

entries.name: flatten
entries.doc: A shape squashed front to back (along z) about z = `at`, to `f` of its depth: a chest, a foot.
entries.code: function flatten(s: Shape, f: number, at?: number): Shape;

entries.name: membrane
entries.doc: A skin of thickness 2r stretched over triangles: a wing's membrane, a fin.
entries.code: function membrane(tris: Vec3[][], r: number): Shape;

entries.name: scales
entries.doc:
A pattern of scales: space cut into staggered cells of size `a`. Gives how
far the point is from its cell's middle (0 at the middle, 1 at the seam) and
a number 0–1 that is the same all over one scale.

entries.name: Creature
entries.doc:
A body builder for procedural creatures: a skeleton, plus a list of simple
shapes (tapered tubes, ellipsoids, flat sheets, and filled cones for things
like flame), each covered in flat surface blobs and weighted to the bones
named on it by distance. The fox (creature.ts) was the first creature and
builds its own way; the frog, elf and dragon are written in this.

Blobs are spread by area, so a part gets its share of `count`; `density`
gives small parts (eyes, claws) more than their share. Lighting is baked into
the color from a fixed light, as for the fox, unless a part is `glow`.

entries.name: Part
BodySpec
Built
rng
entries.code: function rng(seed: number): () => number;

entries.name: boneTail
entries.doc: Where a bone ends in the rest pose: its tail, else its first child's head, else a short way on from its parent.
entries.code: function boneTail(bones: Bone[], i: number): Vec3;

entries.name: shapeArea
entries.code: function shapeArea(s: Shape): number;

entries.name: buildBody
entries.doc:
Builds a creature from its spec with about `count` blobs. The same spec and
seed always give the same creature.
entries.code: function buildBody(spec: BodySpec, count: number, seed?: number): Built;

entries.name: segDist
entries.doc: Distance from p to the segment ab.
entries.code: function segDist(p: ArrayLike<number>, a: Vec3, b: Vec3): number;

entries.name: mirror
entries.doc: Mirrors a point (or a list of them) to the creature's other side.
entries.code: const mirror: (p: Vec3) => Vec3;

entries.name: spots
entries.doc: A cheap, smooth-ish pattern in 0–1 for spots and scales: the same at the same point every time.
entries.code: function spots(p: Vec3, freq: number, seed?: number): number;

entries.name: mix
entries.code: const mix: (a: Vec3, b: Vec3, t: number) => Vec3;

entries.name: Fur
entries.doc:
Fur for a sculpted creature (sculpt.ts): strands grown out of its skin.

The cut creature is a shell of round discs, one per grid cell; textured, it
reads as bricks. Fur is what a Gaussian is good at: every strand here is one
long, thin blob that leaves the skin at a slant and lies the way the coat
runs (`flow`), rooted anywhere inside its cell so the grid never shows. The
shell stays underneath, a shade darker, as the undercoat: it keeps the body
solid where strands part, and the strands' soft tips make the outline soft.

A strand hangs on its root cell's bones with the same weights, so the fur
bends with the body, and it is still a plain blob: files, sprite sheets and
Shape Shifter take it as they take any other.

entries.name: FurryPart
entries.doc: A part of a sculpted creature that may grow fur.

entries.name: quatFromAxes
entries.doc: The rotation whose x, y and z axes are the given (orthonormal, right-handed) columns.
entries.code: function quatFromAxes(x: Vec3, y: Vec3, z: Vec3): Quat;

entries.name: growFur
entries.doc:
Grows `total - shell.blobs.count` strands over the furred parts of `shell`
(cut from `parts`, in the same order), spread by area and `density`, so the
creature comes out at exactly `total` blobs. The same shell and parts always
grow the same fur.
entries.code: function growFur(shell: Sculpted, parts: FurryPart[], total: number): Sculpted;

modules.title: Built things: walls, steps, fences, arcades
modules.doc:
Built things: walls of real bricks, flights of worn steps, fences along a path and arcades cut into
equal bays, each one shape however many pieces it has. Pure numbers and distance functions, so the scene builder
cuts them like any other shape, and each shape's `pieceAt` says which brick, block, post or stone a point is on,
for the `pieces` paint.

Every piece is placed by a rule from the shape's own sizes and a seed (the same seed, the same ruin), and sizes are
fitted so the pieces come out whole: a wall's length is a whole number of bricks (half bricks at the ends of every
other course), a span a whole number of bays, so pillars and posts land exactly at its ends.

The idea comes from Silicon Jungle's Ink Studio built-things kit; this is our own code.

entries.name: hash
entries.doc: A repeatable number in 0..1 from a seed and up to three whole numbers.
entries.code: function hash(seed: number, a: number, b?: number, c?: number): number;

entries.name: noise1
entries.doc: Smooth 1D noise in 0..1 with bumps about `size` apart.
entries.code: function noise1(seed: number, u: number, size: number): number;

entries.name: WallSpec
WALL_BRICK
entries.code: const WALL_BRICK: [number, number];

entries.name: wallPlan
entries.doc: How the bricks of a wall are laid: fitted sizes and which bricks stand.

entries.name: wall
entries.doc: A wall of bricks laid in courses (see WallSpec). `cell` is the grid spacing, so mortar lines are at least a cell wide.
entries.code: function wall(s: WallSpec, cell: number): Shape;

entries.name: fallenBricks
entries.doc: The bricks lying at a wall's foot: each fell from where the top is lowest, lies flat on the ground at a random turn.

entries.name: StepsSpec
steps
entries.doc: A flight of steps, each block its own piece, its nose worn round and its tread hollowed in the middle.
entries.code: function steps(s: StepsSpec): Shape;

entries.name: bays
entries.doc: Where the posts of a span stand: each straight run of the path cut into whole, equal bays, so posts land at every corner.
entries.code: function bays(path: Vec3[], bay: number): Vec3[];

entries.name: FenceSpec
fencePosts
entries.doc: The posts (feet and tops) of a fence, with their leans.

entries.name: fence
entries.doc: A fence of posts and rails along a path: some posts lean, some rails are gone, hang from one end or sag.
entries.code: function fence(s: FenceSpec, cell?: number): Shape;

entries.name: ArcadeSpec
ARCHES
entries.code: const ARCHES: readonly ['round', 'pointed', 'flat'];

entries.name: arcade
entries.code: const arcade: (s: ArcadeSpec, cell: number) => Shape;

modules.title: Formations: crystals, columns, drips
modules.doc:
Formations: shapes that come from a rule rather than placing each one by hand. A faceted crystal and
clusters of them from one root, a geode broken open, basalt columns on a hex grid, stalactites and stalagmites that
join into columns, flowstone down a wall, and icicles under every downward edge of another shape. Pure distance
functions, each with a `pieceAt` for the `pieces` paint.

The idea comes from Silicon Jungle's Ink Studio formations kit; this is our own code.

entries.name: CrystalSpec
crystal
entries.doc: A sided crystal with a pointed end, chipped here and there.
entries.code: function crystal(s: CrystalSpec): Shape;

entries.name: ClusterSpec
clusterCrystals
entries.doc: The crystals of a cluster: the middle one longest and upright, the rest leaning out and shorter the further they lean.
entries.code: function clusterCrystals(s: ClusterSpec): CrystalSpec[];

entries.name: cluster
entries.doc: A cluster of crystals from one root (see clusterCrystals); each crystal is a piece.
entries.code: function cluster(s: ClusterSpec): Shape;

entries.name: GeodeSpec
ColumnsSpec
RISES
entries.code: const RISES: readonly ['dome', 'steps', 'random'];

entries.name: columns
entries.doc: Basalt columns on a hex grid: one shape with a height per column, each column a piece.
entries.code: function columns(s: ColumnsSpec): Shape;

entries.name: DripsSpec
dripPlan
entries.doc: Where each drip falls, and how long its stalactite above and stalagmite below have grown; `joined` when they met.

entries.name: drips
entries.doc: Stalactites hanging from a roof, stalagmites where their drips land, joined into columns where they meet.
entries.code: function drips(s: DripsSpec, thin?: number): Shape;

entries.name: FlowSpec
IcicleSpec
icicles
entries.doc:
Icicles under every downward edge of `host`: its box is looked at from below in columns `every` apart, and where a
column meets the underside of the shape but the column beside it doesn't (or meets it much higher up), an icicle
hangs from that edge. Only the icicles are drawn: give the host its own part.
entries.code: function icicles(host: Shape, s: IcicleSpec, thin?: number): Shape;

entries.name: geode
entries.code: const geode: (s: GeodeSpec) => Shape;

entries.name: flowstone
entries.code: const flowstone: (s: FlowSpec) => Shape;

modules.title: Living forms: trees, cacti, shells
modules.doc:
Living forms: trees grown by space colonization, ribbed cacti, succulent rosettes, bracket fungi,
brain coral, shells wound on a log spiral, horns that curl, antlers with tines and a spine of ribs. Pure numbers and
distance functions: each lights, shadows, grows (on a bone with a `sprout` move) and rigs like any other part.

The idea comes from Silicon Jungle's Ink Studio living-forms kit; this is our own code.

entries.name: TreeSpec
TreeNode
colonize
entries.doc:
Grows a tree by space colonization: points are scattered through the crown, and every point pulls the nearest
branch tip toward it until a branch reaches it. Then each limb is made as thick as what it carries (the pipe rule:
a limb's radius to the 2.5 is the sum of its children's), scaled so the trunk's foot is `r`.

entries.name: tree
entries.doc: A tree grown by space colonization (see colonize): its limbs, and if `leaves` is set a ball that size at each end.

entries.name: CactusSpec
cactusArms
entries.doc: The arms of a cactus: out from the trunk, a bend, and up.
entries.code: function cactusArms(s: CactusSpec): Vec3[][];

entries.name: cactus
entries.doc: A ribbed column of a cactus, with arms that bend up.
entries.code: function cactus(s: CactusSpec): Shape;

entries.name: RosetteSpec
rosette
entries.doc: A succulent: thick pointed leaves set round a spiral by the golden angle, the inner ones short and upright.
entries.code: function rosette(s: RosetteSpec, thin?: number): Shape;

entries.name: BracketSpec
brackets
entries.doc: Bracket fungi: half-round shelves stacked up a trunk, smaller as they go up, flat below and domed above.
entries.code: function brackets(s: BracketSpec): Shape;

entries.name: BrainSpec
brain
entries.doc: Brain coral: a dome worn into meandering ridges and grooves.
entries.code: function brain(s: BrainSpec): Shape;

entries.name: ShellSpec
shellCoil
entries.doc: Points and radii of a shell's coil: a tube wound on a log spiral, growing by the same share each turn.

entries.name: shell
entries.doc: A shell wound on a log spiral; each stretch of the tube is a piece, so `pieces` paints it in bands.
entries.code: function shell(s: ShellSpec, thin?: number): Shape;

entries.name: HornSpec
hornPath
entries.doc: The path of a horn: a curve that turns `curl` times in the plane its first way and the sky make, drifting sideways by `twist`.

entries.name: horn
entries.code: function horn(s: HornSpec, thin?: number): Shape;

entries.name: AntlerSpec
antler
entries.doc: An antler: a main beam that sweeps up, back and round, with tines rising off it, shorter toward the tip.
entries.code: function antler(s: AntlerSpec, thin?: number): Shape;

entries.name: RibsSpec
ribs
entries.doc: A spine of vertebrae with ribs curving out and down each side, widest in the middle: a whale's bones on a beach, a beast's chest.
entries.code: function ribs(s: RibsSpec, thin?: number): Shape;

modules.title: Worn land
modules.doc:
Worn land and layered rock: a height field worn by water and slumping (droplets carve gullies and drop
what they carry in fans; slopes too steep for their rock slide to scree), rock laid down in beds where soft beds wear
back further than hard ones, so ledges, benches and overhangs come by themselves, with hoodoos and natural arches as
presets; cracked mud whose plates curl at their edges; and pebbles along a stream bed, bigger where it runs fastest.

Everything runs once, when the scene is built, from its numbers and a seed: the same seed, the same land. Erosion
has a budget (`MAX_DROPS`, a grid of at most `MAX_GRID` cells a side) so a build stays within a second or so.

The idea comes from Silicon Jungle's Ink Studio erosion kit; this is our own code.

entries.name: Bed
entries.doc: A bed of rock: how thick it is and how hard (0 soft, worn back far, to 1 hard, standing out as a ledge).

entries.name: BEDS
entries.doc: Beds when none are given: soft and hard by turns, a hard one on top.
entries.code: const BEDS: Bed[];

entries.name: bedAt
entries.doc: Which bed a height above the base is in, the beds repeating upward.
entries.code: function bedAt(beds: Bed[], y: number): number;

MAX_DROPS

entries.name: MAX_GRID
entries.code: const MAX_GRID = 112;

entries.name: Land
wornLand
entries.doc: The land, built and worn once per spec (the scene asks again at every detail level).
entries.code: function wornLand(s: LandSpec): Land;

entries.name: terrace
entries.doc:
Heights remapped into steps by the beds they fall in: going up a slope, a hard bed rises as a cliff (most of its
height over little ground) and then holds level for a bench, while a soft bed rises evenly as a slope.
entries.code: function terrace(beds: Bed[], h: number): number;

entries.name: land
entries.doc: Worn land as a shape: its surface from the height field, sides cut straight down, its foot `base` deep. Pieces: the bed a point is in, or -1 where something was laid down (fans and scree).

entries.name: ButteSpec
hoodoo
entries.doc: A hoodoo: a thin butte of soft rock, waisted where its softest beds are, under a hard cap.

entries.name: ArchSpec
MudSpec
PebbleSpec
pebbleList

modules.title: Growers
modules.doc:
Growers: a tree, a coral or a cluster of crystals grown by a branching rule from a seed, so the same
seed always gives the same plant. Pure numbers: `grow` gives the twigs (round-ended sticks, thick to thin) and the
tips, which the scene builder turns into shapes. Each style is a rule: how many branches split from each end, how
far they lean out, how much shorter and thinner each step is, and how hard they pull back toward the sky.

entries.name: GrowStyle
entries.code: type GrowStyle = 'tree' | 'coral' | 'crystal';

entries.name: GROW_STYLES
entries.code: const GROW_STYLES: GrowStyle[];

entries.name: Grower
Twig
MAX_TWIGS
entries.doc: No grower makes more twigs than this, whatever its depth and branches.
entries.code: const MAX_TWIGS = 160;

entries.name: grow
entries.doc: Grows it: twigs from the foot out, and the tips where the last twigs end.

entries.name: growBounds
entries.doc: How far a grower can reach from its foot: half its box's size along x, y and z, and that box's middle.

modules.title: Weather that lands
modules.doc:
Weather that lands: what falls finds the ground actually under it, snow lies in drifts shaped by the
wind and what stands in its way, and frost grows across a pane a branch at a time. Pure and tested.

The idea comes from Silicon Jungle's Ink Studio weather kit; this is our own code.

entries.name: groundUnder
entries.doc:
The height of the first surface met going straight down from `top` at (x, z), or `bottom` if nothing is met. The
shapes' distances are lower bounds, so each step down is as long as the distance says and never steps through.
entries.code: function groundUnder(shapes: Shape[], x: number, z: number, top: number, bottom: number): number;

entries.name: Falling
entries.code: type Falling = 'rain' | 'snow' | 'leaves';

entries.name: fallAt
entries.doc:
Where a falling thing is in its life (0 to 1, starting again each time it falls): `drop`, the share of its fall
done (0 at the top, 1 landed); `lying`, whether it has landed; `size`, from nothing as it appears to nothing as it
goes (snow melts, a leaf fades, rain splashes away quickly). Size is 0 at both ends, so a loop joins up.

entries.name: fallShare
entries.doc: The share of a life spent falling: what a speck's sway is frozen at once it lands.
entries.code: const fallShare: (kind: Falling) => number;

entries.name: DriftSpec
Drift
DRIFT_GRID
entries.code: const DRIFT_GRID = 96;

entries.name: driftField
entries.doc:
How deep snow lies over the ground `under` gives, in a grid: deep where something upwind shelters it (a wall, a
rock, a bank), thin where the wind scours (anything higher than the ground upwind, and steep slopes), thinner on a
path, then smoothed so it lies in soft drifts.
entries.code: function driftField(s: DriftSpec, under: (x: number, z: number) => number): Drift;

entries.name: FrostSpec
FrostBranch
frostPlan
entries.doc:
A frost fern as straight strokes in the surface's plane: main branches curve out from the start, each throwing
side branches at about 60 degrees, every other step on alternate sides, which do the same, smaller, up to three
generations. `t` is when a stroke grows, 0 at the start to 1 at the last tip, by how far along it is.
entries.code: function frostPlan(s: FrostSpec): FrostBranch[];

entries.name: frost
entries.doc: A frost fern lying on a surface (see frostPlan), each stroke standing a little proud of it; pieces are the generations, 0 the main branches.
entries.code: function frost(s: FrostSpec, thin?: number): Shape;

entries.name: drift
entries.code: const drift: (s: DriftSpec, under: (x: number, z: number) => number, thin?: number) => Shape;

entries.name: SceneDoc
entries.doc:
A pixel-art scene written as data: no code, so it can be typed by hand, kept
in a file, or written by Claude from a prompt (docs/scene-descriptions.md).
`checkScene` says what is wrong with one, in words that point at the place;
`compileScene` turns a sound one into what the voxel builder, the bones and
pixel mode need.

Units: about 1 is a small house, and a whole scene is about 4 across. y is up, the ground is y = 0, and the
camera starts on the +z side. Colors are '#rrggbb'.

MistDoc
ShaftDoc
SpeckKind
entries.doc:
What a swarm does: `dust` hangs and twinkles, `embers` rise and fade, `rain` falls fast as streaks, `snow` falls
slowly and sways, `leaves` flutter down, `fireflies` wander and blink, `bubbles` rise and wobble.
entries.code: type SpeckKind = 'dust' | 'embers' | 'rain' | 'snow' | 'leaves' | 'fireflies' | 'bubbles';

modules.title: Sand, snow and goo
modules.doc:
Sand, snow and goo that flow: a small 3D MLS-MPM (moving least
squares material point method, after Hu et al. 2018's 88-line version, in
3D), on the CPU. Each particle carries its place, velocity, affine velocity
field `C` and deformation `F`; each step scatters mass and momentum to a
coarse grid with quadratic B-splines, moves the grid under gravity and the
walls, and gathers it back.

- Sand: Hencky elasticity with a Drucker-Prager yield (Klár et al. 2016), so
  it can't pull and slides once a slope passes its friction angle.
- Snow: fixed corotated elasticity with Stomakhin et al. 2013's plasticity
  and hardening, so it packs where it is pressed and breaks in clumps.
- Goo: soft, and giving way at a small stretch, so it runs out flat and,
  pulled, draws out slowly instead of flying apart.

The box is [0, 1] on each side (the page scales it), the floor y = 0.
Pure and tested.

entries.name: PixelPass
entries.doc:
Pixel mode: the scene is drawn small into a target, and one full-screen pass
turns it into pixel art and scales it up in whole pixels, with no smoothing.

The pass is the GPU twin of `pixelArt` in splat-core/pixel.ts (change one,
change both): alpha cut, glow from bright pixels, nearest palette color in
OKLab with a Bayer dither, edge lines inside the scene, an outline on the
empty pixels that touch it, and a sky behind. It runs once per art pixel,
into `art`, which keeps display (sRGB) color so a palette color is stored
exactly; the screen then gets a plain copy, scaled up. The art of the frame
before is kept too: a look with `steady` reads it so a pixel between two
palette colors does not flip from frame to frame.

modules.title: Pixel art
modules.doc:
The 2D half of Splat to Sprite: everything that happens after the splat has
been rendered. Pure functions on RGBA byte arrays so they can be unit tested
without a GPU.

Pipeline per frame:
  supersampled render → box downsample → alpha cut → palette (+dither) →
  stray-pixel cleanup → outline

entries.doc:
One frame of a scene to pixel art, the CPU twin of the live pixel pass
(change one, change both). `f` is the scene drawn small: straight sRGB.

  alpha cut → glow (bright pixels light their neighbors, and empty pixels
  beside them) → edge lines (the darker side of a jump in color) →
  palette + dither → outline on the empty pixels that touch the scene →
  sky on the rest, if the look has one

`before` is the art of the frame before, for a look with `steady`: where it
holds a palette color that is nearly as close as the best one, that pixel
keeps it. `parts` is the scene's map of parts for a look with `parts`: the
same view with every part in its own flat color (alpha 0 where there is none).

modules.title: Level of detail
modules.doc:
Level of detail per actor: a creature far away or small on screen draws a
share of its blobs, each grown to cover for the ones left out, so it costs
less to draw and looks about the same.

Which blobs stay is fixed per blob by `lodRank` (a hash of its index), so a
creature thinning out loses the same blobs every time and keeps the rest:
nothing flickers as the share drifts. A kept blob's covariance is divided by
the share kept (each axis grows by 1/√keep), so the covered area stays about
the same for the surface discs creatures are cut from.

The GPU (`deformBlob` in engine.ts) and the CPU twin (`SplatWorld.deformCPU`)
use the same hash; change both.

modules.title: Cuts and paint
modules.doc:
Shape edits: cut or paint every blob inside a sphere or a box, live, without
rebuilding anything. The GPU applies them as it moves the blobs (a cut blob
gets no size, as level of detail leaves one out) and as it colors them (a
painted blob's own color is mixed toward the paint before any light).
Edits are tested against where a blob is now, in world space, so a box
that cuts a creature's head off keeps cutting as the head moves through it.

This file is the CPU twin (`editAt`), also used to bake edits into blobs for
a file (`bakeEdits`). The GPU side is `editsAt` in engine.ts; change both.

entries.name: SplatDepth
entries.doc:
A depth map of a scene drawn by the engine, for post effects (fog, outlines,
focus): every pixel's distance in front of the camera, in scene units, in
all three channels of a half-float target, and 0 where nothing was drawn.
The target also carries a depth texture, for passes that want the usual
kind (ordinary meshes write it; blobs, being see-through, do not).

Splats have no single depth: a blob fades out from its middle. Here each
blob counts as a hard disc out to where it has faded to a sixth (as in the
map of parts), and the frame's own sort leaves the nearest disc on top. So
draw it right after the frame's own render, with the same camera: it reuses
that frame's moved and sorted blobs (`SplatWorld.hold`) and costs one more
draw, nothing more.

Ordinary meshes draw their own depth with a stand-in material; lines and
points (grids, helpers) are left out.

entries.name: SKIN_EXTENSION
entries.doc:
Rigged splats in a .glb.

The blobs are a KHR_gaussian_splatting primitive (POINTS, with SCALE,
ROTATION, OPACITY and the degree-0 color as extra attributes), so any
viewer that knows that extension shows the creature. The rig uses only
standard glTF: JOINTS_0 and WEIGHTS_0 on the same primitive, a skin, joint
nodes, and animation channels on those nodes.

What glTF doesn't say is how a skinned *splat* turns, since a blob has a
rotation and a shape as well as a position. Our extension,
BLOBSCAPE_gaussian_skinning, says so: blob centers follow the usual linear
blend, and each blob's rotation is the weighted average of its bones'
rotations. It's listed as used, not required, so viewers that don't know it
still load the file, and most will show the creature standing still. The
full rule is written up in docs/rigged-splats.md.

Morphs are standard glTF morph targets on the same primitive (POSITION
deltas, animated as the mesh node's `weights`), and our second extension,
BLOBSCAPE_gaussian_morphs, adds what a splat needs beside its center: a SHAPE
attribute per target (the morph's local 3×3 map minus identity, morph.ts) and
which targets are in-betweens of one morph. Viewers that know glTF morphs but
not the extension move the centers right and leave the shapes as they were.
entries.code: const SKIN_EXTENSION = "BLOBSCAPE_gaussian_skinning";

modules.title: Rigged models to splats
modules.doc:
A rigged model to splats, keeping its rig: an ordinary skinned glTF (a .glb from Blender, Mixamo or
a game kit: triangles, JOINTS_0/WEIGHTS_0, a skin and its animations) read into our bones and clips, then its
surface covered in flat blobs that hang on the same bones with the weights the mesh gave its corners. Pure: the
page decodes texture images and hands them in as `Texture`s.

Our bones have no rest rotation: a bone is its head, posed by a turn about it. A glTF joint carries any rest
frame, so each frame of a clip is read as what the skin does, not what the nodes say: joint j's skin matrix is
S = G·IBM (its world matrix now times its inverse bind matrix), which takes the bind pose to the posed one. Its
linear part is our bone's world turn (times its scale) and it carries the bind head (where IBM⁻¹ puts the joint)
to where the joint is now. Local turns, offsets and sizes follow from those, so the blobs land where the mesh's
vertices would.

entries.doc:
Reads a skinned .glb: the first mesh node with a skin, its triangles in the bind pose with colors and texture
coordinates, the skin's joints as our bones (parents first), and every animation sampled as our clips.

entries.doc:
The model as rigged splats: `count` flat blobs scattered over its triangles by area (the same seed gives the same
blobs), each lying on its triangle, colored from the vertex colors or the texture at that point, and hung on the
bones the triangle's corners hang on, weighted by how near each corner is. Bones and clips come with it, fitted
to `height` when given.

modules.title: Dragon
modules.doc:
A dragon, standing, facing +z, about eight units nose to tail: 43 bones.
Its body is cut the way the pixel scenes are (sculpt.ts): every scale, tooth
and horn ring is a shape or a pattern on one, lit and shadowed once, and
weighted to the bones so the neck and tail still curve. Its wings are skin
stretched between an arm and three finger bones, so the membrane follows
the fingers as they spread and fold.

Its fire is bones too: a chain of six from inside the mouth. In the rest
pose the flame is built FLAME times smaller than life, hidden in the mouth,
so a file opened elsewhere shows a dragon with its mouth shut; breathing
fire grows the first fire bone by FLAME (a scale key, which glTF has) and
the chain unrolls and flickers. Nothing about it is a particle system.
